gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the MV7+'s XLR output is passive and, in Shure's words, 'XLR audio is not affected by software settings', so Auto Level, the denoiser and the other MOTIV processing only work over USB. Shure's XLR sensitivity (-55 dBV/Pa) is 22 dB below its USB figure (-33 dBV/Pa).
standout_why: I checked itechguides.com (rank 8), which names MV7+ and PodMic USB in its title, and thetoolshelf.com (rank 3). Neither says the MV7+ or PodMic USB processing is USB-only. Thetoolshelf says 'the processing needs the app' but never ties that to the USB connection. Itechguides gives an XLR sensitivity and gain warning only for the SM7B (-59 dBV/Pa, more than 60 dB of preamp gain), not for any hybrid mic. ChatGPT's own answer lists 'Auto gain: Yes' and 'real-time denoising' for the MV7+ and sells these mics on 'the ability to upgrade to an audio interface later', but doesn't say those features stop on XLR. I could not read either cited MusicRadar page (both came back with only the title), so this score is based on the uncited rivals. The finding could be partly covered there.
decides: The usual reason to buy a USB/XLR mic is to move to an interface later. On the XLR path the MV7+ is a passive dynamic mic at -55 dBV/Pa with none of its onboard processing, which is the feature behind its top-pick price and its 'convenience' slot. A shopper who plans to switch to XLR should compare the mics as plain dynamics, where Samson rates the Q9U's XLR sensitivity at -57 dBV/Pa, only 2 dB lower. The MV7+ pick holds only for someone who stays on USB.

findings.label: XLR output type and software processing
findings.value: Passive XLR output; 'XLR audio is not affected by software settings'
findings.source_title: Shure MV7+ user guide, 'MV7+ Outputs' page (ManualsLib copy)
findings.note: The manual says 'Passive XLR output: Connect to XLR mixers and interfaces' and 'Note: XLR audio is not affected by software settings.' MOTIV Mix settings, which include Auto Level, Real-time Denoiser, Digital Popper Stopper, compressor and limiter, therefore don't reach the XLR signal. Shure's own guide at shure.com/en-US/docs/guide/MV7+ only loads with JavaScript and returned no body text, so I used the ManualsLib copy of the same guide.

findings.label: Sensitivity, XLR vs USB-C (1 kHz, open-circuit voltage)
findings.source_title: Shure MV7+ user guide, specifications page (ManualsLib copy)
findings.note: The XLR figure is 22 dB lower (-33 minus -55), so on XLR the interface preamp has to supply gain the mic adds itself over USB. The same page lists frequency response as 50 Hz to 16,000 Hz, XLR output impedance as 350 Ω at 1 kHz, and max SPL (USB-C) as 128 dB SPL.

findings.label: Where Rode places the APHEX processing
findings.value: Rode describes it with the digital USB output only: 'The digital USB output features RØDE's ultra-low-noise, high-gain Revolution Preamp' alongside 'powerful APHEX digital signal processing'
findings.note: The product page links the APHEX processing to the USB output but never says outright whether XLR gets it. The specifications section was empty when fetched, so I took no sensitivity or frequency figure from Rode.

findings.label: XLR and USB sensitivity, and Samson's claim about XLR output level
findings.value: XLR -57 dBV/Pa (1 kHz, 'Max Sensitivity'); USB -16 dBFS/Pa (0 dB gain, 1 kHz); Samson says it 'provides enough output to work with any mixer or audio interface without the need for external amplification'
findings.note: The XLR rating is 2 dB below the MV7+'s -55 dBV/Pa. Samson calls the low-cut and mid-presence switches 'onboard sound shaping options' but doesn't say whether they affect the XLR output. Other specs on the page: 50 Hz to 20 kHz, 250 Ω impedance, USB 24-bit up to 96 kHz.
